newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Some 17 countries ready to go to Congo, but money short.
newsitem.headline: Some 17 countries ready to go to Congo, but money short.

text.p: About 17 countries, mainly from Africa, this week voiced interest in sending troops or other staff to the Congo Republic but money to pay for the operation is still not forthcoming, U.N. officials said.

Many nations are concerned that the off and on fighting in the Congo Republic could spread to other countries, particularly across the river to the former Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The United Nations wants to organise a multi-national force that could eventually turn into a U.N. peacekeeping operation.
"We understand that Senegal has offered to lead the force which is one essential ingredient that had been lacking," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said on Tuesday.
But he said "there continue to be problems of logistics and it remains to be seen what level of political commitment there might be in the Security Council."

U.N. sources said that African countries expressing an interest in the Congo force were Algeria, Botswana, Ivory Coast, Gabon, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Mali, Niger as well as Senegal. In Asia, the countries included Bangladesh, India and Pakistan. And from Europe, Belgium, France, the Netherlands and the Ukraine have offered some support operations.
But these countries still have to spell out precisely what help they would offer.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and his special envoy for the region, Mohamed Sahnoun, have proposed an advance force of about 1,000 troops outside of the U.N. structure in an effort to organise it quickly. They want this force eventually to be increased and approved as a U.N. operation.

But diplomats said the entire venture was still tenuous and questioned whether the United States would approve or help underwrite the operation in light of Congress' reluctance to pay U.N. arrears as well as support any new missions.

A peacekeeping force would be financed by all U.N. members whereby a multinational force would need voluntary funds from the participants or other interested countries. In either case authorisation from the 15-member Security Council is needed to give the operation international legitimacy.

The current conflict in Congo Republic, which has left hundreds of civilians dead, erupted on June 5 when President Pascal Lissouba tried to arrest his rival and immediate predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso during efforts to disband private militias ahead of elections.

Cease-fires have been declared since then, with eight African countries helping in the negotiations. But sporadic fighting continues. Both sides want a peacekeeping force to secure the airport, the main supply route for weapons.
